content: Otomycosis, a fungal infection of the external ear, is commonly treated with topical antifungal agents, particularly those in the azole class. The purpose of this review was to assess the efficacy and safety of topical azole treatments for otomycosis. A systematic search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane ENT Register, CENTRAL, Ovid MEDLINE, and others, up to November 11, 2020. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving adults and children with otomycosis, comparing topical azoles to placebo, no treatment, other azoles, or different formulations of the same azole. A minimum follow-up period of two weeks was required for inclusion. The primary outcomes assessed were clinical resolution (defined as the proportion of participants achieving complete resolution between two and four weeks post-treatment) and significant adverse events. Secondary outcomes included mycological resolution and other less serious adverse effects. The certainty of evidence for each outcome was evaluated using the GRADE approach. Four studies involving 559 participants from Spain, Mexico, and India were included. Three studies enrolled both children and adults, while one study included only adults. The duration of otomycosis symptoms was not consistently reported across studies. Mycological resolution was reported in only one study. The studies compared different types of topical azoles or different formulations of the same azole (e.g., cream versus solution). No studies compared topical azoles to placebo or no treatment. Comparison 1: Clotrimazole versus other azoles (eberconazole, fluconazole, miconazole) Three studies compared clotrimazole to other azoles. The evidence is highly uncertain regarding whether clotrimazole differs from other azoles in achieving complete clinical resolution at four weeks (risk ratio [RR] 0.80, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.59 to 1.07; 3 studies; 439 participants; very low-certainty evidence). The anticipated absolute effects were 668 per 1000 for clotrimazole versus 835 per 1000 for other azoles. One study conducted a safety analysis and reported no significant adverse events in either group. However, the evidence remains very uncertain regarding differences in safety between clotrimazole and other azoles (no events in either group; 1 study; 174 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Clotrimazole may result in little or no difference in mycological resolution at two weeks (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.96 to 1.06; 1 study; 174 participants; low-certainty evidence). Clotrimazole may also result in little or no difference in the occurrence of less serious adverse events at two weeks (36 per 1000 for clotrimazole versus 45 per 1000 for other azoles; RR 0.79, 95% CI 0.18 to 3.41; 1 study; 174 participants; very low-certainty evidence). Comparison 2: Bifonazole cream versus bifonazole solution One study compared bifonazole 1% cream to bifonazole solution. The evidence is very uncertain regarding whether bifonazole cream differs from the solution in achieving clinical resolution at two weeks (RR 1.07, 95% CI 0.73 to 1.57; 1 study; 40 ears; very low-certainty evidence). Bifonazole cream may result in less mycological resolution compared to the solution at two weeks post-treatment, but the evidence is very uncertain (RR 0.53, 95% CI 0.29 to 0.96; 1 study; 40 ears; very low-certainty evidence). Five out of 35 patients experienced severe itching and burning with the bifonazole solution, while no such adverse effects were reported with the cream (very low-certainty evidence). Authors' Conclusions No studies were identified that compared topical azoles to placebo or no treatment. The evidence is highly uncertain regarding the effects of clotrimazole on clinical resolution, significant adverse events, or other non-serious adverse events when compared to other azoles (eberconazole, fluconazole, miconazole). There may be little or no difference between clotrimazole and other azoles in terms of mycological resolution. Similarly, the evidence is very uncertain regarding the comparative efficacy and safety of bifonazole cream versus solution. The generalizability of these findings may be limited due to the narrow range of ethnic backgrounds represented in the included studies.
